name: Zoe Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Lowfield, nine hundred acres of wheat, barley and oilseed rape, with a few fields of beans to rest the soil. This time of year I'm on the drill or the sprayer, and on wet days I'm in the grain store turning the heaps and checking moisture readings. I start at seven, after I've dropped the girls at the bus stop on Station Road, and I finish when the light goes or the job's done, whichever's later.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you done it, and what came before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Three years. Before that I did twelve years as a care worker, nights mostly, and my back and my head both gave out at about the same time. Lowfield needed someone for harvest, and my partner Dev's cousin manages it, so I got the chance. I'm still the one who gets told twice how to calibrate the sprayer, which at forty-three is humbling.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the quiet in the cab, and the smell of rape in flower, even though half the village says it gives them hay fever. What wears me out is the money. Dev drives parcel vans, and with two of us on low pay and a mortgage, one broken boiler is a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful and leave it there. I already ask one of those AI chat things to explain a spray label now and then, because the labels are written by lawyers. It hasn't changed my wages one penny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a better search engine is a small win for someone like me who's still learning. It's like having a patient colleague who doesn't sigh when you ask the same thing twice. But it's not paying the boiler man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Much the same as now. I'd do my spraying certificate properly this winter, using the AI thing to quiz me at the kitchen table. And I'd try to put fifty a month away, which we never manage, but I'd try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly pleased, even, because it helps me catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fifty a month and never manage it. What usually eats it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: School trips, shoes, the car. Last month it was Priya's school trip to the coast, sixty-five pounds, and you can't be the one parent who says no. So the fifty went, like it always goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Lowfield uses this stuff, apart from you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Raj, Dev's cousin, uses it for the grain market reports, he says it saves him an hour a morning. The older lads won't touch it. Bert says if he wants to talk to a machine, he'll talk to his lorry.

S0.say: I'd say it's useful and leave it there. I already ask an AI chat tool to explain spray labels, but it hasn't changed my wages at all.
S0.think: A better search engine is a small win for someone like me who's still learning, like a patient colleague who doesn't sigh. But it doesn't pay the boiler man.
S0.do: Studies for her spraying certificate this winter, using an AI tool to quiz herself at home. Tries to save fifty a month, though school costs usually swallow it.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little pleased because it helps her catch up.
S0.quote: It's like having a patient colleague who doesn't sigh when you ask the same thing twice.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe is a careful, dry talker who already uses AI tools a little and finds them helpful for learning. Money is the steady background worry, shown by a sixty-five pound school trip wiping out her savings for the month. There's no gap between her public and private views here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should make sure young people still get a start, through proper paid training schemes. Farming is already an old person's job, the average farmer near us is past sixty. If firms stop taking beginners, the whole thing gets older still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd count myself lucky to have got in when I did. I was the beginner they took a chance on. If this had happened five years ago, Dev's cousin might have said no, sorry, the combine does it now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to stop being the beginner, basically. Get my spraying and forklift tickets, learn the grain store's moisture system inside out, and ask for a small raise in spring with the certificates on the table. I'd also start a little notebook of what I know that a machine wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a way I can handle. Slow gives you time to learn, and I can learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in the notebook so far, if you started it today?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which corner of Long Meadow floods after heavy rain, and why you never drill it before the tenth of October. Which buyer pays on time. That old Bert, who drives the grain lorry, will wait an hour for you if you give him tea with three sugars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask for a raise. Have you ever done that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Never, not once, in care or here. I'd write it down first and practise it in the car. I know I'd say sorry at least twice, which Dev says is my whole problem.

S1.say: I'd say young people still need a start, through proper paid training schemes. Farming's already old, and if firms stop taking beginners it gets older still.
S1.think: I count myself lucky to have got in when I did. If this had happened five years ago, I might have been told the machine does it now.
S1.do: Gets her spraying and forklift certificates and learns the grain store's moisture system fully. Asks for a small raise in spring with certificates in hand, and starts a notebook of local know-how.
S1.feel: Uneasy but manageable. Slow change gives her time, and she trusts herself to learn.
S1.quote: Old Bert, who drives the grain lorry, will wait an hour for you if you give him tea with three sugars.
S1.fieldNote: Her instinct is to make herself less of a beginner, step by step, which fits a steady adapter. The notebook idea came from her, and the contents are knowledge only someone on the ground would have. She supports public training schemes but plans her own way up without waiting for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to stop arguing and sort out a safety net before the layoffs, not after. I'd share posts about it. I did nights in care homes, I know what happens when help comes too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't touch Lowfield much. The farm office is one woman, Sandra, two days a week, and she might go, which would be sad. Where it bites is Dev, because the parcel company is already trying route software that plans everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Dev to look at his heavy goods licence now, while he's still on a wage, so he's not stuck in a van that a computer schedules. We'd put the course on the credit card, which I hate. And I'd offer to take on some of Sandra's simpler jobs, the grain passports and the weighbridge tickets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, mainly for Dev. He takes things in quietly and then goes very quiet for a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that week look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd fix things. When his last firm cut his routes he regrouted the whole bathroom in three nights. The girls would notice before I did, and Asha, the younger one, would just go and sit next to him on the floor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate using the credit card. How much is on it now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About eleven hundred, from the boiler last winter. We pay forty a month off it and it barely moves. Putting a driving course on top would feel like stepping into deep water to fix a leak.

S2.say: I'd say the government should build a safety net before the layoffs, not after. I'd share posts about it, because I saw in care work what happens when help comes too late.
S2.think: It barely touches Lowfield, though Sandra in the office might go. The real risk is Dev's parcel driving job, where route software is already coming in.
S2.do: Gets Dev to start his heavy goods licence while he's still earning, paid on the credit card. Offers to take on some of the office's simpler paperwork herself.
S2.feel: Anxious, mostly for Dev, who goes quiet when things go wrong.
S2.quote: When his last firm cut his routes he regrouted the whole bathroom in three nights.
S2.fieldNote: The worry moves from her job to Dev's, which she sees clearly. She is both public-minded and practical: she wants a safety net but makes her own family plan in case it doesn't come. The detail about Dev regrouting the bathroom said a lot about how her family copes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the people who own the AI shouldn't keep it all. Tax the shares, tax the house price jump, and use it to pay for retraining and care. I'd go to meetings about it, and I don't usually go to meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be in the lucky half, which feels odd to say. But house prices booming is no good to us, we've got the one house and nowhere to move. And if Lowfield is sold to some investment fund flush with share money, I don't know who I'd be working for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and work hard, honestly. I'd talk to Dev about whether he could come onto a farm too, at harvest at least. And I'd see the bank about fixing the mortgage before anything jumps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy for me, anxious for everybody else. It would feel like watching a flood from the one dry hill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you picture losing out, in your town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister, Meera, works at an insurance office in town, and her husband's a surveyor. They have the nice house and the holidays. I can imagine her ringing me, asking if Lowfield needs anyone, and that would turn everything upside down between us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would that turn things upside down?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've always been the sister who struggles. Meera paid for Priya's school shoes once and I cried in the shop toilets afterwards. If she needed me for a job, I honestly don't know who I'd be.

S3.say: I'd say the people who own the AI shouldn't keep all the gains. Tax shares and the house price jump, and use it for retraining and care.
S3.think: I'd probably be in the lucky half, which feels odd to say. But a house boom does nothing for us, and if an investment fund bought Lowfield I wouldn't know who I worked for.
S3.do: Stays put and works hard. Asks Dev about joining farm work at harvest, and sees the bank about fixing the mortgage.
S3.feel: Uneasy for herself and anxious for others, like watching a flood from the only dry hill.
S3.quote: It would feel like watching a flood from the one dry hill.
S3.fieldNote: Her mood went down a step here, unusually, because physical work is spared. Her politics are clear and she'd act on them more than usual. The family role reversal with her better-off sister seemed to interest and unsettle her in equal measure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms need rules: who owns them, who gets retrained, who checks they're safe around people and animals. I'd push for the farm workers' union to have a real seat at the table. Not just a photo with a minister.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, grain is the easiest farm work to automate. The tractors already steer themselves by satellite, and a robot that loads the drill and checks the store would finish off what's left of my job. I'd be gone inside two years, I reckon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Lowfield straight out whether they'd keep someone to look after the machines, and ask to be trained for it. I'd use the AI tools every evening to learn the robot side, the error codes, the basics. And I'd ring the care agency, because care work might still be people, even with robots, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel like I'd climbed a ladder and someone had taken it away while I was on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said care work might still be people. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half. The card says robots go into care homes too. But I've held a dying man's hand at three in the morning, and I don't believe a robot does that, or if it does, I don't want to know the world where it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the girls?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, mostly, that Mum's job might change and we'll be all right because we always manage. Priya's thirteen, she'd see straight through anything else. I'd tell Asha it's like when the bus route changed, annoying, but we found another way.

S4.say: I'd say robots on farms need rules on ownership, retraining and safety around people and animals. The farm workers' union should have a real seat at the table, not just a photo.
S4.think: Grain is the easiest farm work to automate, because the tractors already steer themselves by satellite. I'd be gone inside two years, I reckon.
S4.do: Asks Lowfield to train her to look after the machines and studies robot basics with AI tools every evening. Rings her old care agency as a fallback.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like someone took away the ladder while she was on it.
S4.quote: I've held a dying man's hand at three in the morning, and I don't believe a robot does that
S4.fieldNote: She shows the sharp jump expected for hands-on work, from uneasy to alarmed. Her plan is both to move up to machine care and to fall back on care work. She admitted she only half believes care work would be safe, and her answer about the dying man was the most emotional moment of the interview.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one. What would help is paid retraining that starts before the job goes, not a leaflet after. If someone paid me a wage while I learned to fix the machines, I'd be first in the queue.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they know that isn't written down anywhere. Every farm runs on things like which corner floods. When those people go, that goes too, and nobody notices until a drill's sunk in Long Meadow.

headlineQuote: I'd feel like I'd climbed a ladder and someone had taken it away while I was on it.
portrait: Zoe Gupta is 43 and three years into farm work at Lowfield, a grain and oilseed farm, after twelve years as a night care worker. She lives with her partner Dev, a parcel driver, and their two daughters, with a mortgage and almost nothing saved. She already uses AI tools a little to learn, and in the early scenarios she plans to climb step by step with certificates and a notebook of local know-how. Her worry shifts to Dev as office work changes, eases slightly when only thinking work is hit, and turns to alarm when robots reach grain farms, where she expects to be gone within two years.
biggestWorry: The robots scenario, because grain work is easy to automate and she'd lose the ladder she's only just climbed.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining that starts before the job goes, especially a wage while she learns to look after the machines.
